parts.title: Campus Conversation: A Full Class
script: Narrator
Listen to a conversation between a student and an employee at the registration office.
Woman
Hello. How can I help you today?
Man
Hi. I want to take Biology 101 next semester, but the website says the class is full.
Woman
Let me check. Yes, Biology 101 has fifty students. That's the limit for the room.
Man
Oh no. I really need this class. It's required for my major.
Woman
Don't worry. There are a few things you can do. First, you can put your name on the waiting list.
Man
A waiting list? How does that work?
Woman
If a student drops the class, the first person on the list gets the place. Right now there are only three names on the list, so your chances are good.
Man
Only three? OK, that sounds better than I thought.
Woman
Also, there's a second section of Biology 101. It meets on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, from six to eight. It still has ten open places.
Man
Evenings... Hmm. I work at a restaurant on Tuesday nights.
Woman
I see. Then the waiting list is probably the best choice for you. You can also email the professor. Sometimes professors let one or two extra students in.
Man
That's a good idea. Who teaches the class?
Woman
Doctor Patel. Her email is on the biology department website.
Man
Great. Can you add my name to the waiting list now?
Woman
Sure. I just need your student ID card.
Man
Here it is. Thank you so much for your help.

parts.title: Academic Lecture: Why Do Volcanoes Erupt?
script: Narrator
Listen to part of a lecture in a geology class.
Professor
Good afternoon, class. Today we're going to talk about volcanoes. What are they, and why do they erupt?
Professor
Let's start with the inside of the Earth. Deep under the ground, it is very, very hot. It's so hot that rock melts. This melted rock is called magma.
Professor
Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it. So, slowly, it moves up toward the surface. Sometimes it collects in a big space under a mountain. We call this space a magma chamber.
Professor

Now, magma has gas in it. Think of a bottle of soda. When you shake it, the gas pushes hard. When you open it, the soda comes out fast. A volcano works in a similar way. When the gas pressure becomes too strong, the magma breaks through the ground. That is an eruption.
Professor
When magma comes out of the ground, we give it a new name. We call it lava. So remember: under the ground, it's magma. Above the ground, it's lava. Students mix these up on tests all the time!
Professor

Volcanoes can be dangerous, but they also help people. Volcanic soil is very rich. Farmers near volcanoes can grow a lot of food. For example, many farms near Mount Etna in Italy grow fruit and vegetables in this soil.
Professor
Scientists watch active volcanoes very carefully. They measure small earthquakes and gas around the mountain. These signs can tell them an eruption may come soon, so people can leave in time.
Professor
OK. Next time, we'll look at the different shapes of volcanoes. Please read chapter seven before class.

o: How farmers grow fruit in Italy

What volcanoes are and why they erupt

He says, 'This melted rock is called magma.'
